Reproductive output in the Grey butcherbird is modest, a pattern reflecting its life as a persistent, year-round territorial resident. This conservative annual schedule, with just one clutch annually, results in a relatively slow breeding tempo compared to many smaller, multi-brooded passerines that inhabit similar woodlands. Successful fledging, therefore, represents a considerable investment in a small number of offspring per year.

The nestling period is energetically taxing for the parents, who must deliver a steady supply of insects and small vertebrates to the brood. This high food demand is likely the ecological factor that limits the species to a single successful brood per season, as the parents would be unable to sustain the provisioning effort for two consecutive rounds of growth in the same breeding window.

The larger male body size may confer advantages in agonistic encounters over prime foraging territories, while the lighter female mass might reduce flight costs during the critical period of egg formation and incubation. These contrasting adult masses highlight how intra-specific variation in body size is a key parameter shaping the species' overall life history and behavioral ecology.
